node.name: Writing as Struggle: Process after AI (Session 3) | Author as Metaphor: Personal and Collective Style in Generative Prose: A Talk and Workshop with Dennis Yi Tenen
node.descriptionText:
Dennis Yi Tenen (English and Comparative Literature, Columbia University) is the author of "Literary Theory for Robots" and "Plain Text: The Poetics of Computation." He will be introduced by John Durham Peters (English and Film and Media Studies, Yale University).

Abstract: When, if ever, does a thought become inalienably mine? In this talk, we will try to capture that vague feeling of ownership that nevertheless emerges from writing in groups or with generative AI. Case studies of syndicate and institutional authorship will frame the question historically, with particular attention to the Stratemeyer Syndicate and reports “written” by the National Transportation Safety Board. Viewed from the perspective of collective labor, recent developments in machine learning invite us to reconsider several persistent assumptions about personal voice and collective style. Questioning these assumptions opens up new directions for research in literary history, with implications for academic policy and scholarly practice. In the workshop that follows, we will explore collective style experimentally, through group dynamics and specific prompting strategies.

Coffee will be provided before the session, from 2:00-2:30 p.m.

Note: If you wish to attend other sessions, please be sure to sign up separately as we have capacity limits. For the full schedule, see the workshop website: https://campuspress.yale.edu/struggle/schedule/

node.name: Big Brothers Big Sisters
node.descriptionText:
Big Brothers Big Sisters requires a unique application process to be fully prepared to work with New Haven Public School Students. Please read below!


Since 1904, Big Brothers Big Sisters (BBBS) has helped children realize their potential and build their futures through meaningful mentorship. BBBS Connecticut and Dwight Hall are partnering to provide mentorship to the children at Truman School in New Haven.

We are seeking caring Yale students to become "Bigs" - mentors who support the dreams of, listen to, and empower students at Truman School. By becoming a "Big", you will join a tight-knit community that fosters education and collaboration, develop friendships with other mentors, and most importantly, create a lifelong bond with a Truman School student.

Please note that this position requires a weekly commitment on Thursdays from 2:30-5pm (3-4:30pm without transportation time) for the 2024-25 academic year. Transportation will be provided by the program. Limited spots are available and decisions are made on a rolling basis.

Below is the process of applying to this position:
Complete the BBBS application here: BBBS Application.
Once you have submitted this application, submit the Yale Connect form: https://cglink.me/2dA/s95475
We will then review your application. Once it is approved, you will be able to register for this opportunity under the "Service Opportunities" page in Yale Connect, which can be found here: Service Opportunities.
Approving applications typically takes one week. If you have any questions, please email j.navarro@yale.edu. We look forward to reading your applications!

node.name: Fall 2026 Environmental Humanities Graduate Symposium
node.descriptionText:
Please join us for the Fall 2026 Environmental Humanities Graduate Symposium on the afternoon of Thursday, November 12, 3:30–5:00pm, in HQ 134 (320 York Street). Graduate researchers from across the university will share and discuss work related to the environmental humanities. A reception will follow the presentations. 

Symposium Presentations:
 
Seth Embry (Architecture): “Coppice Urbanism: Investigating a Model of Responsive and Adaptive Reconciliation Ecology through the Design of Urban Forestry Systems”
 
Vincent Calvagno (History): “Streams for Mills’: Water and Property in Colonial New England”
 
Lisa Kennedy (American Studies): “The Walleye War Continues: Settler Colonial Grammars, The Conservation Establishment, and Enduring Anti-Treaty Sentiment”
 
Stefano Piantino (Italian and Early Modern Studies): “That deep within me / was your perilous law? Montale’s Whirpool-Wea: for a poetics of aquatic unattainability”
 
Lightning Talk:
 
Francis Ayitey (African Studies): “Beyond Global Climate Frameworks: Leveraging Indigenous Knowledge for Climate Governance and Sustainable Development in Ghana”
 
Reception: 5:00pm
 
Yale Environmental Humanities gratefuly acknowledges the financial support of The Edward J. and Dorothy Clarke Kempf Memorial Fund and the 320 York Endowment/FAS Humanities Division.

node.name: Thriving Across Neurotypes: Building Connections for Academic and Career Success
node.descriptionText:
Join us for a session exploring how neurodiversity shapes our experiences in academic and professional environments. Dr. Wendy Xiao Herman, a neurologist specializing in neurodevelopmental conditions such as autism, will discuss how neurodivergent traits are an integral part of humanity and especially common in academic communities. Participants will explore their own neurodiversity, better understand those around them, and consider how greater awareness can foster more inclusive and connected communities as well as promote academic and professional success.

Speaker:
Wendy Xiao Herman '17 PhD (Interdepartmental Neuroscience Program), '18 MD

This event is part of the "Where Do I Go From Yale?" series (WDIGFY).

node.name: Making the Invisible Visible: Exploring Identity, Perspective, and Power Through Art
node.descriptionText:
Through guided observation by Kerri Davidson, MD-PhD student, participants will explore how our perspectives shape the way we understand patients, colleagues, and ourselves. By shifting viewpoints, both literally and figuratively, we will reflect on professional identity, implicit assumptions, power dynamics, and the ways our experiences influence how we see and are seen in medicine.

This intimate, facilitated workshop offers an opportunity to step outside our usual clinical and academic environments, engage in meaningful conversation, and consider how art can help us see ourselves and others more fully.

node.name: Hatha Yoga (11/12)
node.descriptionText:
Join Karmen in the Yale Schwarzman Center Dance Studio (located on the lower level of YSC) for hatha yoga with an emphasis on the South Asian roots of the practice. Classes will include all areas of yogic study, practiced through movement, meditation, mantra, mudra, and breathwork, and are meant to be a guide for your personal practice.

Yoga mats will be provided but you are more than welcome and encouraged to bring your own. Please bring flexible clothes, a water bottle, and an openness to slowing down your breath and mind for 60 minutes! 

If you realize you cannot attend, please cancel your registration so that students from the waitlist may join. 

The Good Life Center is committed to making our events accessible to everyone. At your request, yoga instructors may be able to offer modifications for certain poses during your yoga class. If you require an accommodation or service to fully participate, please contact goodlifecenter@yale.edu.

node.name: How to Find Scholarly Articles
node.descriptionText: Are you ready to find scholarly articles thoroughly and efficiently – without relying on Google Scholar or a chatbot, while also avoiding paywalls ($$)? Learn strategies to find and access scholarly articles from Yale Library.
node.descriptionHtml:
Are you ready to find scholarly articles thoroughly and efficiently – without relying on Google Scholar or a chatbot, while also avoiding paywalls ($$)? Learn strategies to find and access scholarly articles from Yale Library.  

Attendees will learn how to:  

  • Use Articles+ to access scholarly articles for free (like Google Scholar but better)  
  • Identify specialized article databases (JSTOR, ScienceDirect, etc.)  
  • Access online and print journals from Yale Library  
  • Place a request for articles through interlibrary loan  

Workshop Incentive Program: Any student who attends at least 3 library workshops this semester will be eligible to receive a FREE Yale Library tote bag. Learn more.
